title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene (613469) on chromosome 10q24.2.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24, within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified.
checks.explanation: The abstract places HPSE2 only within 10q23-q24. The more precise band 10q24.2 is standard gene-location nomenclature, so it is accepted.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression (Wang et al., 1997). Patients have an 'inverted' facial expression, in which they appear to be crying when they smile (Derbent et al., 2009). Daly et al. (2010) described facial grimacing when attempting to smile and failure of the urinary bladder to void completely despite a lack of anatomic bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage. Affected individuals present with enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction resulting from neurogenic bladder (Wang et al., 1997). They often have reflux of infected urine from the bladder to the upper renal tract, with a risk of kidney damage and renal failure (Daly et al., 2010), and some severely affected patients become hypertensive and progress to end-stage renal disease (Derbent et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, one of which was consanguineous (first cousins). The patients had peculiar facies and gestures when smiling and crying. They also had hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the urethra in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal trabeculated bladder with diverticula associated with severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes. Elejalde (1979) suggested that the syndrome represents alteration of the facial and urinary developmental fields.

paragraphs.text: Between 1965 and 1986, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) saw 36 children with enuresis and urinary tract infection in association with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. Urologic workup showed characteristic findings of mild neuropathic bladder in all cases, and most patients had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen in 20 selected patients with urofacial syndrome, using a combination of homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling with one patient pool and three control pools of unaffected relatives. Of 36 randomly chosen markers, D10S677 was linked to and associated with UFS: patients had a significant excess of homozygosity compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)), and allele frequencies differed between the patient pool and the control pools. The authors then analyzed 10 additional markers flanking D10S677 and covering a 22-cM region. All 31 patients were homozygous for 2 closely linked markers, D10S1726 and D10S198, located approximately 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, whereas only 12% of unaffected relatives were homozygous for both markers (P less than 10(-19)). Several patients were heterozygous at the 2 markers immediately flanking D10S1726/D10S198, D10S1433 on the centromeric side and D10S603 on the telomeric side. These recombinations placed the UFS gene within a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition, which can help with early assessment and treatment and may lead to a better prognosis. Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) recommended urologic evaluation for individuals with 'inversion' of facial expression because of the clear association between this distorted facial expression and neuropathic bladder with resulting damage to the genitourinary tract. Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) stressed that early diagnosis has important consequences for the management and prognosis of the urinary problems. Derbent et al. (2009) recommended that physicians consider the syndrome in any patient who presents with dysfunctional voiding, particularly in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.
